title: Policy Enforcement Playbook for Routing & Control Plane
content:
Purpose and scope
- Working playbook: where to evaluate and enforce access policies in the request path for the Redwood routing/control plane. Focus: authz hooks, ABAC/RBAC mapping, multi-region failover, and low-latency constraints.
- Audience: platform-engineering architects, infra engineers, SREs, and security reviewers.

Goals
- Define discrete enforcement points (fast-path vs slow-path).
- Minimize p99 add-on latency while preserving strong auditability and policy correctness.
- Ensure predictable behavior across hosted/dedicated/private modes and across regions.

High level enforcement zones (candidate list)
1) Edge ingress / API gateway (region-local):
   - Responsibilities: initial authentication, token validation, high-level authorization decisions (simple allow/deny based on token scope, account state).
   - Good for: coarse-grained RBAC checks, rate-limits, geo-based deny lists, quick rejects.
   - Tradeoffs: limited context (no model-level attributes, no long project metadata) unless enriched from cache.

2) Routing layer / proxy middleware (per-request):
   - Responsibilities: policy evaluation using enriched attributes (project, environment, model tier, deployment tags, customer contracts), route selection, region affinity.
   - Provides hooks for pre-route authz and post-route verification.
   - Good for: ABAC decisions that require request attributes and routing metadata.

3) Control plane policy engine (central, strongly consistent):
   - Responsibilities: source of truth for policies, policy authoring, versioning, rollout. Provides API for other enforcement points to query evaluate.
   - Good for: complex policy logic, policy change management, audits.
   - Tradeoffs: cannot be in hot path for per-request decisions unless backed by cache or fast evaluator.

4) Serving runtime guard (node-level enforcement):
   - Responsibilities: last-mile enforcement — deny/transform requests if they violate runtime constraints (quota, model access, sensitive model flags).
   - Good for: protecting model execution surface, enforce slow-changing constraints.

5) Fallbacks and region-specific enforcers:
   - Responsibilities: local enforcement when central control plane unreachable; enforce safe-fail policies (deny or degrade to limited mode).

Policy evaluation patterns
- Fast-path cacheable allow/deny: cache token->principal->roles and allowlist lookups in edge/proxy with TTLs tuned for security vs performance.
- Attribute-based evaluation (ABAC): attributes used: principal_id, org_id, project_id, env, region, model_id, model_tier, dataset_sensitivity, token_scopes, request_origin_ip, time_of_day.
- Role-based fallbacks (RBAC): map RBAC roles to coarse capabilities when attribute evaluation not possible. Roles: viewer, developer, service-account, ops, infra-admin, auditor.
- Decision model: policies authored as allow-when-any(conditions) with explicit deny precedence. Support obligations: transform, redact, route-to-quarantine.

Authz hook interfaces (proposed)
- Pre-route hook (proxy): synchronous, low-latency, returns {allow|deny|challenge, metadata}. Should support quick context enrichment and short-circuit denies.
- Pre-execute hook (runtime): synchronous or fast async with timeout; verifies quotas, model-level restrictions, and sensitive-data flags.
- Post-route audit hook: async, writes detailed decisions and evidence to audit log for later correlation.
- Control plane evaluation API: REST/gRPC interface for complex evaluations and policy lookup. Must support batch evaluation for fanout requests.

Multi-region considerations
- Placement of enforcement: prefer region-local fast-path evaluation using cached policies and attribute snapshots to avoid cross-region latency.
- Policy propagation: use versioned policy bundles with signatures; runtime/proxy validate signature and version.
- Stale-policy handling: define safe defaults (deny-by-default for deny-sensitive policies; allow-readonly for non-critical).
- Failover behavior: if central policy service unreachable, allow cached allow decisions for time window X for critical traffic only, otherwise fail closed. X should be configurable per customer/tier.

Performance & reliability constraints
- Target: authz check adds <3ms median and <10ms p95 on the routing fast-path.
- Use local caches, edge token introspection caches, and compact policy evaluation engine (wasm or optimized interpreter).
- Instrumentation: per-decision latency, cache hit rate, decision outcome histogram, policy eval errors.
- SRE playbook: if authz p95 crosses threshold, temporarily switch to permissive read-only mode for non-critical customers with alert to security on-call.

Audit and observability
- Every enforcement decision logs: request_id, principal, attributes used, policy_id, decision, timestamp, evaluation_latency, enforcement_point.
- Retention: security tier logs 1y, default 90d, with export hooks to customer(s) for Private deployments.
- Correlate with trace IDs for full request replay.

Policy lifecycle and tooling
- Authoring: Confluence + policy-as-code in repo. Policies stored as versioned YAML with tests.
- CI: unit/eval tests with sample attributes and negative/positive cases.
- Rollout: canary rollout of policy versions across regions; allow rollback.
- Governance: require approvers for deny-high-impact policies.

Threat model notes
- Token replay from another region: mitigate via short-lived tokens and region-bound claims.
- Policy poisoning: signed policy bundles and audit trail for changes.
- Lateral privilege escalation via mis-routed attributes: ensure attribute provenance checks and signatures.

Open questions / TODOs
- Attribute propagation: what is canonical source for project metadata? (control plane vs customer metadata service) TODO: map sources and TTLs.
- Decision caching invalidation: define strong invalidation signals when policies change.
- Fast-path evaluation engine: wasm vs embedded evaluator. Benchmark plan needed.
- How to represent obligations (transform/redact) consistently across proxies and runtime.

Testing checklist
- Unit tests for policy authoring (positive/negative).
- Staging canary: deploy new policy bundle to single region and run fuzz traffic.
- Chaos: simulate central policy outage and validate fallback behavior.
- Performance: microbench authz with 10k qps, measure p50/p95.

Immediate next steps (owners)
- Priya: draft policy bundle schema and example ABAC rules (due 2026-03-12).
- Diego: prototype pre-route hook in routing-proxy with cache and signed policy bundle validation (P0 spike, 2 weeks).
- Hannah: design metrics and alert thresholds for authz latency and cache staleness.
- Marcus: security review of fallback deny/allow defaults and audit retention constraints.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally pragmatic: separate fast-path decisions from control-plane policy logic. We prefer signed, versioned bundles that let edge/proxy act autonomously under clear safe-fail rules.
- Comments inline are welcome; document will be iterated into an RFC after prototyping.

References and links
- Confluence: CONFLUENCE-PLN-243 (policy model draft)
- Jira: JIRA-INFR-872 (routing-proxy authz spike)
- Repo: github.com/redwood-inference/routing-proxy#45

Quick list of sample policy examples (sketch)
- deny if principal.sso_disabled == true
- allow if token.scope contains model:generate and project.billing_status == active
- deny if model.sensitivity == high and principal.role != infra-admin
- quarantine if model.tier == experimental and request.origin == external

---
End of playbook draft.
